name: Buckwheat
short: Food allergen: can cause anaphylaxis, including a fatal case in an 8-year-old girl after eating buckwheat then exercising (case report). Severe reactions are rare; also occupational asthma.
text: Reviews describe buckwheat as a cause of IgE-mediated allergy, from urticaria, rhinoconjunctivitis and asthma to life-threatening anaphylaxis, after eating it, handling or inhaling the flour at work, or sleeping on buckwheat husk pillows. A 2021 review estimated the prevalence of buckwheat allergy at 0.1-0.4% in Japan, Korea and buckwheat-eating areas of China and 2-7% among allergy-clinic patients, with 4-60 cases of buckwheat-related anaphylaxis per 100,000 school children in Japanese and Korean school studies, and concluded that severe reactions are rare; it reported clinically relevant cross-reactivity with peanut, latex, coconut, quinoa and poppy seed. A 2025 review notes that buckwheat is often included in unlabelled gluten-free foods. Case reports include the death of an 8-year-old girl from food-dependent exercise-induced anaphylaxis after eating buckwheat noodles and then swimming, a 57-year-old man with biphasic anaphylaxis who lost consciousness twice on the same day, and a case series of six food workers with occupational buckwheat allergy (asthma, rhinitis, contact urticaria), three of whom later had anaphylaxis after eating food containing buckwheat. Buckwheat also contains phototoxic fagopyrins: a systematic review found reliable toxicity data lacking and judged seeds, flour and teas generally safe in normal amounts, but said diets made up largely of buckwheat sprouts, herbs or flowers, or fagopyrin-rich extracts, may cause fagopyrism (a phototoxic reaction). No interaction data were found in the cited sources.
